title: Latency vs Throughput
subtitle: Measure response time and capacity without confusing them
objectives: Tell latency and throughput apart, and know which fix applies to which
Recall the order-of-magnitude latency numbers and do back-of-envelope math
Reason with percentiles and explain why fan-out turns rare slowness into the norm
Explain how utilization, queueing, and Little's Law connect throughput back to latency

exercises.title: Latency measures duration; throughput measures completion rate
exercises.body: Latency is elapsed time from a request's start to its response, usually measured in milliseconds. Throughput is completed work per unit time, such as requests per second. A service can add workers and complete more concurrent requests while each request still follows the same execution path.
exercises.note: Replicas leave each request's network and processing work unchanged. When existing workers are saturated, added capacity can shorten the queue and reduce total latency.

exercises.prompt: Users in London call a service hosted in Virginia. Move an identical service instance closer to those users.
exercises.beforeStatus: NETWORK ROUND TRIP · approximately 80ms to Virginia
exercises.afterStatus: NETWORK ROUND TRIP · approximately 10ms within London
exercises.result: Distance removed about 195ms of network delay
exercises.why: Geographic routing shortens propagation distance, so it can reduce network latency for each request. It does not optimize slow application code or database work that still runs after the request arrives.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: Users in London call a service hosted in Virginia. Move an identical service instance closer to those users. Place London users, London. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: London users → London. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Geographic routing shortens propagation distance, so it can reduce network latency for each request. It does not optimize slow application code or database work that still runs after the request arrives.

exercises.prompt: One worker completes a fixed, independent job in 100ms. The queue is empty. Which change raises maximum throughput without reducing one job's 100ms processing latency?
choices: Make the same worker finish each job in 50ms
Run a second identical worker in parallel
Make each job twice as large
exercises.why: With enough independent work, two workers can each complete ten 100ms jobs per second, giving about 20 jobs per second together. With an empty queue and unchanged work per job, each job still spends 100ms processing. Parallel capacity increases throughput while service time stays fixed.

exercises.prompt: ______ is the time for one request to complete; throughput is how many complete per second.
exercises.why: Latency measures elapsed time for one operation, commonly in milliseconds. Throughput measures completed operations per unit time, so a system can change one metric without changing the other.

exercises.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Max data per second the link can carry

exercises.why: Latency measures one request’s duration, throughput measures completed work per second, bandwidth caps data transfer per second, and round-trip time covers travel to a destination and back. A different bottleneck can keep achieved throughput below available bandwidth.

exercises.prompt: Your servers have plenty of headroom — nothing is queueing. Which of these actually reduce LATENCY for a single request? Select all.
choices: Caching the result so the work is already done
Moving the server geographically closer to the user
exercises.why: Caching removes repeated work, geographic proximity shortens propagation distance, and query optimization reduces processing time. With no queueing, extra servers increase parallel capacity but do not shorten the path of one request.

exercises.prompt: You double your server count. Users still say each page takes 2 seconds. Why didn't it get faster?
choices: The new servers need a restart
More servers add throughput (capacity to serve more users), not lower per-request latency
Servers always fix latency — something is misconfigured
DNS is caching the old servers
exercises.why: Doubling server count increases the number of requests that can run concurrently. When requests were not waiting for capacity, their network and processing path remains two seconds; extra servers reduce latency only when they remove queueing.

exercises.prompt: Your API serves 10,000 requests per second, and each one takes 200ms. Which is the throughput?
exercises.why: The completed-work rate is 10,000 requests per second, so that value is throughput. The 200ms value measures how long an individual request takes and is therefore latency.

exercises.title: Storage and network operations differ by orders of magnitude
exercises.body: Representative latency scales are about 1 nanosecond for an L1 cache hit, 10² nanoseconds for main memory, and 10²–10³ microseconds for a same-datacenter network round trip. Convert units before comparing: 1 microsecond is 1,000 nanoseconds.
exercises.note: These are capacity-planning estimates, because hardware and topology change exact values. The exponent is usually more useful than a precise benchmark from another system.

exercises.prompt: A checkout performs four independent 100ms service calls one after another. Run them concurrently without changing the work each service performs.
exercises.afterStatus: DEPENDENCY TIME · about 100ms · one parallel wait
exercises.result: Elapsed latency fell while total downstream work stayed the same
exercises.why: Independent calls can overlap, making elapsed time approach the slowest call instead of their sum. Parallel fan-out increases concurrent load and failure exposure, so cap concurrency and assign deadlines.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: A checkout performs four independent 100ms service calls one after another. Run them concurrently without changing the work each service performs. Place Checkout, 4 dependencies. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Checkout → 4 dependencies. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Independent calls can overlap, making elapsed time approach the slowest call instead of their sum. Parallel fan-out increases concurrent load and failure exposure, so cap concurrency and assign deadlines.

exercises.prompt: Roughly how much slower is reading from main memory (RAM) than from the CPU's L1 cache?
exercises.why: An L1 cache access is roughly 1 nanosecond and a main-memory access is roughly 100 nanoseconds, giving an order-of-magnitude ratio near 100. Exact timings vary by processor and access pattern, but the hierarchy remains operationally significant.

exercises.prompt: Reading from main memory (RAM) takes roughly how many nanoseconds?
exercises.why: A main-memory access is on the order of 100 nanoseconds. This estimate supports scale comparisons: cache-friendly access can avoid memory stalls whose cost is many processor cycles, although exact latency depends on hardware and locality.

exercises.prompt: A network round trip between two servers in the SAME datacenter takes roughly how many microseconds?
exercises.why: A same-datacenter network round trip is commonly on the order of 500 microseconds. Serialization, network-stack processing, switching, and queuing make this much slower than a local memory access even within one facility.

exercises.prompt: Match each operation to its rough order of magnitude.
exercises.why: The matched values establish a latency hierarchy: L1 cache near 1ns, RAM near 100ns, a random solid-state drive read near 100µs, and an intercontinental round trip near 150ms. Moving work across each boundary can dominate the computation itself.

exercises.prompt: One same-datacenter network call takes roughly as long as 5,000 RAM reads. What system-design risk does this reveal?
choices: RAM should be replaced with network storage
Many serial service calls can dominate request latency
Network calls are effectively free inside one datacenter
Every service call requires exactly 5,000 reads
exercises.why: One same-datacenter call consumes a time budget comparable to about 5,000 RAM reads. A design that replaces local access with many serial service calls can therefore add substantial latency even when every remote service is healthy.

exercises.prompt: Why bother memorizing these order-of-magnitude numbers at all?
choices: To impress people in code review
To do back-of-envelope math and reject a bad design in seconds — without building it
They're required by the HTTP spec
They're only useful for embedded programming
exercises.why: Order-of-magnitude values expose infeasible designs before implementation. For example, 10,000 serial calls at 0.5ms each contribute about five seconds of network wait, so the request path must reduce or parallelize those calls.

exercises.title: Latency percentiles expose slow requests hidden by the mean
exercises.body: Mean latency divides total elapsed time by request count, so a small slow tail can have little effect on the result. A percentile sorts request latencies: p50 is the median, while p99 is a threshold that 99% of measured requests complete at or below.
exercises.note: A page that fans out to many dependencies has more chances to encounter at least one tail event, so end-to-end p99 can be much worse than each dependency's p99.

exercises.prompt: Your dashboard says average latency is 100ms — healthy. Users are furious that the app is slow. How can both be true?
choices: The average hides the tail: a small share of requests could be taking 5+ seconds
exercises.why: A small slow tail can coexist with a healthy average because the average collapses the full distribution into one value. For example, many 50ms requests can numerically mask a small set taking several seconds, even though those users experience the slow requests directly.

exercises.prompt: Match each metric to what it actually tells you.

pairs.right: 50% complete at or below this threshold
95% complete at or below this threshold
99% complete at or below this threshold

exercises.why: p50, p95, and p99 are latency thresholds at or below which 50%, 95%, and 99% of measured requests complete. Roughly 1% are slower than the p99 value; p99 is a boundary value, not the set of slowest requests. The average combines every latency and is sensitive to extreme outliers.

exercises.prompt: Your p99 latency is 2 seconds. What does that mean?
choices: 99% of requests are faster than 2 seconds; the slowest 1% are worse
exercises.why: A p99 of two seconds means 99% of observed requests completed within two seconds and the slowest 1% took at least that long. At high request rates, that percentile can still represent many slow requests.

exercises.prompt: At 10,000 requests/second, how many requests per second land in your p99 tail (the slowest 1%)?
exercises.why: One percent of 10,000 requests per second is 100 requests per second. Converting a tail percentile into an absolute rate reveals how many slow experiences the system produces under its actual traffic.

exercises.prompt: A page fans out to 100 independent calls. The chance that all 100 are fast is about 37%. Roughly what fraction of page loads contain at least one slow call?
exercises.why: The prompt supplies that all 100 calls are fast for about 37% of page loads. The complementary 63% therefore contain at least one slow call, showing how independent tail risks accumulate across large fan-out.

exercises.prompt: Which of these genuinely help tame tail latency? Select all.
choices: Hedged requests: send a duplicate and take whichever answers first
exercises.why: Hedging can complete from a faster duplicate, timeouts cap dependency wait, and reduced fan-out lowers the number of opportunities for a straggler. Running at 100% utilization increases queueing and can worsen the slow tail.

exercises.prompt: You're writing a latency SLA for your service. Which metric should it be written against?
choices: The average — it's the most representative
A high percentile like p95 or p99 — it bounds the worst experience users actually hit
The minimum — it shows what's possible
The maximum — the absolute worst case
exercises.why: A high percentile such as p95 or p99 expresses a measurable bound for nearly all requests while still responding to recurring tail problems. An average can hide that tail, and a single exceptional event can make the maximum unstable as an operating target.

exercises.title: Near saturation, queueing delay raises request latency nonlinearly
exercises.body: Response latency includes queueing time plus service time. When arrival rate approaches a component's completion capacity, normal bursts arrive faster than work can finish, so the queue grows. Requests then wait behind earlier work even when their own processing cost is unchanged.
exercises.note: Operating headroom absorbs bursty arrivals and variance in service time. At sustained demand above capacity, the queue grows until requests time out or load is rejected.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: Near saturation, queueing delay raises request latency nonlinearly
exercises.why: Response latency includes queueing time plus service time. When arrival rate approaches a component's completion capacity, normal bursts arrive faster than work can finish, so the queue grows. Requests then wait behind earlier work even when their own processing cost is unchanged. Operating headroom absorbs bursty arrivals and variance in service time. At sustained demand above capacity, the queue grows until requests time out or load is rejected.

exercises.prompt: Your server handles requests comfortably at 50ms when it's half busy. You push it to 99% utilization. What happens to latency?
choices: It stays around 50ms — the work per request didn't change
It drops, because the CPU is warmed up
It explodes: requests queue behind each other, and wait time grows non-linearly
exercises.why: At 99% utilization, arrivals frequently find the server busy and wait in a queue. As utilization approaches full capacity, small bursts or service-time variation produce disproportionately large queueing delay, so latency can rise even when work per request is unchanged.

exercises.prompt: Little's Law says: concurrency = throughput × latency. Your service handles 500 requests/second, each taking 0.2 seconds. How many requests are in flight at any moment?
exercises.why: Little’s Law gives concurrency as throughput multiplied by latency: 500 requests/second × 0.2 seconds = 100 in-flight requests. If latency rises at constant throughput, the in-flight population and pressure on pools rise proportionally.

exercises.prompt: Little's Law again: 200 requests/second, each taking 0.5 seconds. How many requests are in flight?
exercises.why: Little’s Law gives 200 requests/second × 0.5 seconds = 100 concurrent requests. This value estimates the worker, connection, or request capacity needed to sustain the stated rate and latency.

exercises.prompt: Writes arrive slowly at 10/sec. A batcher flushes when it collects 100 writes or after a timeout. Compared with immediate writes, what tradeoff does this policy create?
choices: Throughput goes up, but an individual write's latency goes up — it waits for the batch to fill
exercises.why: Batching amortizes fixed setup, logging, or commit cost across multiple writes, which can raise throughput. At only 10 arrivals/sec, reaching 100 takes about 10 seconds, so early writes wait for the size threshold or timeout and have higher latency. A producer-supplied full batch would not incur this fill delay.

exercises.prompt: You're designing 'send message' in a real-time chat app. Slide toward what you'd optimize.
exercises.why: A chat sender is waiting for visible confirmation, so batching directly adds user-visible delay. Sending promptly prioritizes latency; background ingestion can accept batching delay when higher throughput is more valuable.

exercises.prompt: Select the bottleneck that caps this pipeline's maximum throughput: Load Balancer (10k rps) → App servers (2k rps) → Cache (50k rps) → Database (5k rps).
exercises.why: Every request crosses the 2,000-rps app tier, the lowest-capacity stage, so it limits the pipeline even though later components are faster. Sustained arrivals above 2,000 rps build a queue before the app servers and eventually cause timeouts; accelerating the cache does not remove that failure.

exercises.prompt: Users report the site is slow. Average latency looks fine at 80ms. CPU sits at 95%. p99 latency is 4 seconds. Diagnosis?
choices: Nothing's wrong — the average is healthy
The servers are near saturation, so queueing is exploding the tail: most requests are fine, but the p99 is brutal. Add headroom or cut work per request
exercises.why: At 95% CPU, bursts queue behind nearly saturated workers, producing a four-second p99 while many requests still keep the average low. Adding headroom or reducing per-request work addresses the queueing mechanism.

exercises.prompt: A video-call service can encode 100,000 frames/sec overall, but each frame waits 900ms before encoding. Which metric is failing the interactive product?
exercises.why: The fleet's total frame rate is high, but one frame waits almost a second. Interactive quality depends on end-to-end latency and its tail, not throughput alone.
